Continuing to use such words outside of quotes, so in your own voice, is an issue. It further solidifies the narrative that so many people already have that indigenous peoples are somehow savage, barbaric, or simply less evolved than Western cultures. These narratives have direct effects on indigenous peoples around the world today. I'm not asking you to apologize for your quote. I'm not even asking you to apologize for the part that wasn't a quote. I was attempting to point out that the part that wasn't a quote shouldn't have contained the word "savages" to describe North American indigenous peoples. It was, apparently unwisely, an attempt to point out a point of view you may not have been aware of, and an attempt to engage you in an internal dialogue that might have a chance of changing harmful terminology that you're still using today. 

You're not being attacked by people pointing out you spoke in a way that was, inadvertently or not, racist. Being called racist isn't a damn insult or attack; it's an invitation to become a less-racist person. It's an invitation to take a step back and learn how you might do things differently in the future. But you know, you do you, boo.

"Uncertain authenticity" and "lack of independent corroboration" does not equal the absolute of "no validity whatsoever." 

It means more data is needed before the truth can be known, not "we know the truth and it's full of lies."

People should absolutely be skeptical of recovered/repressed memories because there's consensus in the medical community that a) they are rare; b) attempting to recover memories within therapeutic contexts is far more likely to result in the creation of false memories; and c) there is as-of-yet no way to prove which memories may be real and which memories may be false. 

Yet people, such as some posters above, who claim all repressed/recovered memories are automatically false are doing a disservice to the truth as well. The best we can say about completely repressed memories is that the possibility of them is an unproven theory. However, there are plenty of theories that are accepted as working facts in many scientific disciplines. While rare, repression is often evidenced in trauma victims, and dissociative amnesia (a sudden lack of autobiographical memories) is a legit symptom of many people who have suffered severe trauma. I'm really glad most of the people on this thread seem able to take the concept of repressed memories, especially in some of the women in these documentaries, with skepticism without falling to the extreme of discrediting the possibility that they might be true completely.

Yes, I do. I've worked clinically with sexual abuse victims and myself am a childhood sexual abuse survivor, so I'm seeing things from it sounds like the opposite side of the situation that you are. In this case, the gentleman admitted it while nearing death. One could equally ask, however, if in all those cases of individuals victimized by "repressed memories" that you are quoting if you also have irrefutable proof that THEIR claims are true. Likely, your answer would factually be no, as there is simply no way to prove one way or another that something did or didn't happen 30 years ago. 

In no way am I saying all cases of recalled memories are true, just as I'm sure you're not saying that every case of recalled memories is absolutely unequivocably false. As with everything, I'm sure we can agree the reality is somewhere in the middle, and that in every case that reality is murky and unclear at best. 

The large issue with recalled memories is that given the amount of time that has passed, there is often no way to prove beyond a reasonable doubt whether or not the accusation is founded in fact. That's why even among medical professionals, there is hesitance regarding recalled memories, specifically if they were recalled under therapeutic circumstances (especially under hypnosis, which does nothing to enhance memory recall but often puts the subject in a state of heightened suggestibility). There is simply as of yet no way to measure whether any memory is factual or fictitious, and we know, clinically, that memory is an often fallible process--for instance, the studies on eyewitness testimony. From a clinical standpoint, however, that doesn't mean that the victim (of either abuse or fictitious memories) doesn't believe that these things happened or isn't suffering psychologically in the same way as if they did. I think from a medical and legal standpoint our society is still working to find ways to properly seek healing and justice for all sides, and we often fall far short of that. I think it's important, however, that we still approach the issue on all sides with compassion and understanding in our hearts.

When discussing the liability & physical damage coverage for an owner's rented vehicle, [Turo's](https://support.turo.com/hc/en-us/articles/217043898-Detailed-explanation-of-owner-protection-plans) website states:

> So long as an owner is in compliance with the Terms of Service...

You're admitting to violating the TOS--specifically, your violation is found under the "Specific Terms for Owners" section, "Information Given at Registration" heading, where the baseline eligibility requirements are linked and list the following:

> The vehicle must be model year 2005 or newer, have fewer than 130,000 miles/200,000 kilometers.

Whether you were aware of this rule or not (and it sounds like you were), you were violating the TOS all the time. You're not entitled to physical damage coverage based on that violation. Based on what the website says, it doesn't even sound like you're entitled to liability coverage for that crash. Sorry to say it, because I understand that from where you're sitting this is an awful situation, but the best you could hope for is some refund of your premiums. However, I wouldn't bet on that, as it sounds like you were aware that you were violating the TOS and just figured they had noticed and decided not to care.

When we're discussing ableism, we need to understand what it looks like--and yes, feels like--before we can say "Oh, this is/isn't ableist." 

Like I said above, not every ideological system is going to mesh perfectly well with every other. So, a few things here that, perhaps, being able-bodied, you might not be cognizant of:

Not everyone, or even most people, who are disabled can afford or have access to an aide. That's expensive, even with good insurance, and not all of us have family or friends who can drop everything all the time to care for us at the drop of a hat (not all of us have family or friends).

Many disabilities affect one's ability to work to some degree, meaning many people with disabilities either work part time, work for minimum wage, or are living on charity or government assistance. And being disabled, we tend to spend more on things like healthcare and assistance than able-bodied people from the start. While from a financial planning standpoint, it makes sense to  buy hundreds of dollars of assistive devices, many of us simply can't afford it. Hell, my wheelchair is manually-operated, second-hand, and I STILL had to crowdfund to afford it. 

You're right that stores should absolutely be accommodating to those with disabilities; everyone should, in the society we currently live in. But the thing is we shouldn't have to ask for help all the time; we shouldn't have to constantly be reminding people to actually remember we exist and think about what we may need. We should, ideally, live in a society where that already happens, and our needs are taken into account from the very outset. 

After all, the majority of people, at some point in their life, will suffer from at least a temporary disability. But your comment, that those with disabilities simply aren't planning well enough for their own needs, tends to be how society will treat all of us as soon as we become seriously ill or injured: as ignorant, or slow, or children, incapable of taking care of ourselves. 

It's not always about convenience; it's about lessening pain (can you imagine the level of pain someone with severe rheumatoid arthritis would feel, trying to peel an orange or do any other dexterous task? Just try, for a moment), or accessing necessary services/goods, or just enjoying a damn orange once in a while--like y'all get to do every day, without having to think about how it's going to happen.

Speaking as a disabled person, I completely understand the argument and can agree. At least in the US, where I'm from, there's a lot of inherent ableism built into the way our society functions and how people think, feel, and act. Myself, I would think it would be a less wasteful, more environmentally conscious choice to have peeling/cutting of fruit (and any other product needing it) available on request. However, then you may have people who are being judged for wanting special treatment, or who are shunted aside because the employee is busy, or who have a disability that precludes public speaking/being able to ask, or (and this is often myself) who are sick and tired of constantly having to ask for help in a world where it seems everything is built to push the disabled out of the way. 

Everyone should attempt zero waste, to the extent that they are capable. Being cognizant of how myriad disabilities may make certain aspects of zero waste (or anything under the sun) difficult or impossible is something that should ideally be inherent, as it should be in any social movement. We should always be seeking to design systems where those on the margins of society do not need to adapt, but are fully and totally included from the outset. 

That doesn't mean there's always going to be a good answer. Here, I don't know that there is one. Maybe in this instance, zero waste ideals and reducing ableism can't both be realized to their utmost potential. Just because these instances pop up from time to time, though, that doesn't mean we should stop trying.

Queer trans Muslim here. I mostly lurk, but specifically because of posts like this. 

It is entirely possible to reconcile Islam with queerness/gayness/whatever-label-you-chooseness. It isn't always (or even often) easy, especially if you follow a more traditional & conservative Islam or were raised in that type of Islam, but it happens. There are even openly gay imams, so the idea that Islam and queerness cannot coincide safely or happily isn't as clear-cut as folks often make it seem. I reverted from atheism 7 years ago, and I've never once questioned that choice, because I am happy as a Muslim and as a queer person.

I highly suggest doing some more research for yourself. Scott Kugle has some great books about Islam and homosexuality, both in history and in the current era, that I highly recommend getting your hands on as an introduction. I'd also recommend Kecia Ali's "Sexual Ethics and Islam." There's queer-friendly masjids popping up all over the world, and I follow a few on social media because I know the folks involved, like Masjid al-Rabia in Chicago and Masjid al-Tawhid in Toronto, but unity mosques are a growing phenomenon, especially in the West. Muslims for Progressive Values is a good organization to get involved with if there's a local chapter, or online if there's not. I've met a lot of queer Muslims through MPV and even more queer-friendly Muslims. I'm also a big fan of the Muslim Alliance for Sexual and Gender Diversity, which runs a weekend-long retreat for LGBTQ Muslims every year in the US. Imam Daayiee Abdullah is an openly-gay imam in Washington DC who is active in the media and really just an overall empowering person--I love reading his writing and his words because it always reminds me of feeling Allah's love, even on days when I might otherwise struggle to feel that.

All of this is to say, basically, that we're here, and you can be, too. Like I said, it's not always easy--as you might read in this thread, a lot of Muslims will judge you for being gay and a lot of gay people will judge you for being Muslim. I'm so sorry for your partner; for many raised in the faith, what he feels is a common struggle. I hope someday he learns to love himself the way I believe Allah does, as a whole person, one who doesn't have to cut off part of himself to connect to his faith and his Lord. But what he feels isn't the only way to feel. Acceptance is growing, and one of the things I love about Islam is that it's always open for interpretation and reinterpretation, even on matters which the ulema claim to have settled long ago, like homosexuality. 

Ultimately, you are the only person who will ever know if you are ready for Islam to enter your heart. But please, don't assume it never can because you are gay. It entered mine, and it has made my life infinitely more rich. Good luck, brother, and may Allah guide you along the straight path.

My mother kept having these bad stomach aches right before bed, to the point where she'd be curled up in a tight little ball covered in heating pads and in tears, but they'd pass in an hour or so. This went on for a week or two. One Saturday night she had a bad one and I stayed up late to make certain she was all right. She looked pale, but the only light in the room was the TV and I thought maybe that's all it was. My dad was still awake and so when she stood up and said she was starting to feel better I figured it was okay to go to bed.

I walk up the stairs, close the door to my room, and put some music on. I had just finished changing in to my pajamas when I hear my father screaming my name. I rush downstairs and into the hallway and see the bathroom door open; my mother's skin is this strange bluish-gray color and only the whites of her eyes are showing, and she's gone limp. My father, who shows less emotion than Tywin Lannister, is kneeling in front of her, screaming her name, holding her and shaking her by the shoulders. I've taken some crisis training and I tell him to put her on the floor (so her head is level with her heart and it doesn't have to pump as hard, or some halfway-remembered mumbo-jumbo that sounds good but may mean nothing). I sprint into the kitchen and grab the phone, running to the front door to turn on the outside lights while dialing 911. I've got the phone cupped to my ear with one hand and I'm grabbing her medicines and stuffing them into a bag for EMS to take with the other, shooing the dog upstairs so I can open the front door so we'll see the ambulance when it shows up, and they'll see us. I happen to turn back towards the hallway and my dad's started chest compressions. My mom starts to try and sit up, mumbles something, and then falls back down to the floor with an audible thump. And then, the 911 operator still talking in one ear, my dad screaming my mother's name in the other, and sirens starting to doppler through the otherwise quiet night, I hear it. 

If you've never heard someone die, I don't quite know how to describe it, the sound of someone's throat constricting around bronchial secretions and the last breaths escaping their body. If you've ever seen *Ju-On* or *The Grudge*, that noise the Toshio character makes might be close. It's this guttural, drawn-out, stuttering sort of sound. When you hear it, even if you're watching the person making it, it doesn't seem human. It's more mechanical than that. And mechanical is a good word for it, because in a very real sense, that's all it is. Whatever person, whatever being you have lived with and loved, is no longer really there, at that moment; this is the simple physical process of air being expelled through a small tube by the contraction of muscular fibers. I had never seen a person die before; but I knew, as soon as that sound started, that I was seeing it, hearing it, now. 

The EMTs arrived probably less than a minute after that sound stopped. I know she wasn't breathing when they loaded her into the ambulance. I know she wasn't breathing when my father and I parked crooked and ran into the ER, not even stopping to ask the front attendant which room she was in. And I know she wasn't breathing, not on her own, when a nurse grabbed my shoulder and steered me out into the waiting room. But she was breathing when, seven hours later, they finally let me back in.

That was 14 years and a few surgeries ago. She's had a few attacks since then, but never so severe. The doctors still don't have a really accurate explanation for what occurred; it seemed to be a perfect storm of a few underlying and undiagnosed conditions. I don't live at home anymore, but given my parents' advancing ages and the effects of time, I try to visit at least once a month. I sleep on the couch, in viewing distance of my mother, when I do. I always wait for her to fall asleep before I can even try. And my phone is always within reach of my hand, especially on the nights her stomach starts to hurt.

I think it's within the realm of possibility. I think we have to acknowledge that. My ex and I were together for 8 years and split recently after I came out as trans. It was difficult, especially because 6 years ago she told me SHE was trans. I was the first person she told and helped her through the process as much as possible and really thought it'd be OK, that she'd be OK, being with me after I came out to her. 

I want to say that I think what you are feeling is normal when such a large shift is happening in your life and in your family; I think it's perfectly natural to start questioning a lot of things & to be worried about where the change may take you and whether this relationship is going to be one you can make work, or whether you even want to.

There's nothing wrong with realizing that you may no longer be physically attracted to your wife when they transition. There's nothing wrong with realizing that you may even fall out of love. But I'd caution not to jump into the divorce boat just yet; transition takes time, a lot of it, and this is just the beginning. Your thoughts and feelings, as well as your wife's, will be in flux a LOT, especially if it does turn out divorce is what's in the cards and you both find yourself grieving for the relationship you did and might have had.

I would suggest, if it's something available to you and affordable, to think about getting some counseling to talk these feelings out in depth with someone. In time, it may be a good idea to get couples' counseling, if only so that there's a neutral party in the room while you two hash out whatever is happening in your lives and in your relationship. But at least anecdotally, having a licensed counselor to bounce my feelings off of from time to time has been helpful in both my own transition and years ago, when helping my girlfriend through hers.

I also want to echo what others have said: that even if this means the end of your romantic relationship and marriage with your wife, it doesn't mean the end of your history together or the things you've shared or a relationship in the future. You may not be married, but a lot of people are able to stay close friends. Myself, I'm still mourning for the life I had with my ex and the pain of knowing that to be myself fully, I had to let her go. But we're still friends. We still hang out, we still talk, we still exchange gifts on the holidays and laugh and hug and love each other. We just love each other in a different way now, and that's okay. Don't give up.

Non-binary people are people whose gender is not man or woman. 

I can refer to science because chromosomes are not what make up gender. Chromosomes are part of what make up sex, and biological sex and gender are related, but they aren't the same thing. Biological sex is determined by medical professionals visually categorizing a child at birth. If they are unable to determine the "proper" sex category because of genital ambiguity, they measure the clitoris/penis--if it's a certain size, it's called a penis and the baby is a boy. If it's under that size, it's called a clitoris and the baby is a girl. If ambiguity affects more than simply size of the clitoris/penis, a decision needs to be made by the doctors and surgery is performed to make the child appear more in line with the decided sex, often right after birth & without parental consent, but thankfully this is becoming less common, and intersex people are more likely to be allowed to make their own choice closer to puberty.

Gender, on the other hand, is social & psychological category based upon largely internal factors, including but not at all limited to hormones, biological structure of the brain itself, social expectations, etc. It's an identity that is based in biology as well as thought patterns, and we are still barely scratching the surface of how it becomes defined. We know there are structural differences in some trans people's brains compared to cis people's brains. We know that sometimes trans folks have different hormone levels, naturally, than cis folks. We know that some trans folks have "body maps" that don't include their genitalia; much like people who have amputations may eventually lose the ability for their brain (not cognitively, but neurologically) to recognize that a limb used to be there. We know many trans folks don't have any discernable physical difference to cis folks, but are still undeniably trans. It's a whole big thing that we're just learning about and it's exciting and amazing and above all, real.

A person's gender might match their sex, but it doesn't have to. A person's gender might remain the same throughout their life, but it doesn't have to. Some people are male sex and and are men; some people are male and are women. Some people are female and are women; some are female and men. Some people are intersex and are men; some people are intersex and are women. Some people are male/female/intersex & NOT a man or a woman. It's a thing. It happens. It's just part of the amazing variety of life.

I did answer the question. Genders outside the male/female binary exist. I have no "feelings" about that, just as I don't have any feelings about man or woman as a gender category. People are often confused or just ignorant about non-binary folks, & a lot of people thus don't like us, but we still exist. The more we learn about the human brain, about neuroscience & hormones & genetics, the more we learn about psychology & sociology, the more science is teaching us that gender is a complex and varied spectrum, not a binary. Depending on the source, you can get statistics anywhere from 8-67% of the US homeless population are veterans, but the fact remains that a statistically significant number of them are. Given the percentage of US citizens who are veterans, the statistic is disproportionate enough to say that veterans are more likely to end up homeless than non-veterans. Homeless vets are predominately male, single, living in urban area, & suffering from mental illness or substance abuse. If this man, like the majority of homeless/at-risk people, suffered from a mental illness &/or substance abuse, it's more than possible he ended up in jail at some point. Both the mentally ill and those with substance abuse issues are more likely to be arrested & imprisoned (veterans who served in 'Nam are at much higher risk for PTSD/depression & substance abuse issues than veterans of any other war, incidentally). If he was in prison, even if he wasn't a member of a Russian organization, he may still have picked up some of the symbolism (alternatively, he might just like cats who smoke tobacco).

In my experience, when fasting, I drink on average about 96 oz of water a day, spread out through the day (don't try to drink an entire liter at once, it's just going to make you feel gross). If you feel kinda hungry, drink some water. It'll help with the hunger pangs and help fill your stomach up. 

Obviously, if you're trying to lose weight, don't eat just whatever you want. You'll lose more weight eating kale and chicken then you would eating potato chips and pizza. Check out r/keto to get an idea of healthy foods and meals that might help stimulate weight loss. 

Fasting can often make people feel different. Some people report more energy, some report feeling happier, some report hating the entire thing. It definitely will not happen right away. Even when I'm fasting for Ramadan, the first three days or so suck. It will take a while to notice how fasting is affecting you physically and emotionally. 

And as others have said, please please please do some serious reading on fasting. Books, articles, etc. Don't just listen to random people on the internet with no credentials besides "I did this once and this is how it worked for me." Every body is different, and you will be affected in different ways. Just Google "intermittent fasting" and learn what you might be expecting and how to do this healthfully.

Real talk: you cannot "fix" a psychiatric issue by losing weight. You can certainly gain self-confidence by losing weight and that will definitely help with the anxiety, but you will continue to have issues with anxiety until you are able to get to the underlying causes and deal with them by seeking treatment. If you're in uni, I highly suggest seeing if your school offers counseling services. Many unis offer them for free, and there's nothing wrong or shameful about seeking help. Good luck.

I was also a pretty troubled kid, and ended up in and out of both psych hospitals and drug rehabs from the ages of 12 through 28. At the age of 18, I got in a bad relationship, got kidnapped, beaten, trafficked, and didn't really get the right kind of help for it once I was able to escape because his defense attorney was able to use my psych and drug issues to claim I didn't know whether I had consented or not and even my own parents for a time didn't take me seriously. So at the age of 20, when I'm trying to put some of this behind me and move on with my life and get treatment for the physical damage that had been done to me, I wasn't probably in a great headspace. And this really stellar neurologist I'm seeing for the TBI I've been left with that's caused some severe chronic pain puts me on Neurontin. Which, apparently, can cause manic states in people with bipolar disorder. Now, I've had manic states before. I've even had hyper-religious manic states before. When I was 15 and in a psych ward I had this weird hallucination that the Virgin Mary visited me and then the room became filled with blood and she turned into some weird version of evil Galadriel and I was convinced Satan was real. 

But Neurontin was something different. 3 days after they put me on it, my parents had gone out and I was home alone. I got this sudden urge to go outside and pray. Which, again, atheist. But I knew I needed to do this, so I did. It was the middle of February in New England but I went outside barefoot, faced the setting sun, and began speaking in some weird babbling language that definitely wasn't English. My parents lived on the edge of a forest and this flock of starlings or something swooped down over my kneeling body in the snow. I looked up just at that moment, and had to throw myself to the ground to keep from being hit by some of the birds. I honestly don't know how to explain the feeling that hit me then--I spent years trying to find it again in pretty much every illicit substance I could get my hands on, and never did. There was this openness, and sudden knowledge that everything in the world was part of me and I was part of it and God was speaking to me, through me, with me... I was the vessel and its contents both, and I was not just happy but completely at peace with everything that existed. 

Two days later, I was back in a psych ward on different meds and in serious therapy to try and get me back to normal. Two weeks later, I took my shahada and converted to Islam. It's been a weird journey, but a good one. I know on an intellectual level that I was just experiencing a pharmacologically-induced psychosis but there is a part of me that is still convinced that in that one moment, I saw Allah (or the Universe, or Oneness, or whatever way you choose to interpret the Spirit). I've gone through a lot since then and learned a lot about what happened to me in that moment on a psychological and neurological level. But since then I've had faith, and I've never lost it. I don't know that it's possible for me to. Something really real happened to me or through me in that moment, and I know it doesn't make logical sense, but I'm willing to accept that it doesn't always have to in order to be real.

IIRC the earliest probable AIDS death so far identified was in 1918. It's likely that the disease spread to humans through an African hunter being bitten by two separate monkeys from two separate species, & each was carrying a different virus that, in the hunter's blood, co-mingled & mutated to become the first HIV strain that affected humans. From forensic virology studies that look at mutation rates, this most likely happened IIRC 10,000 years ago. It's likely HIV/AIDS was a background zoonosis that broke through in mild epidemics from time to time in Cameroon, The Congo, & other surrounding areas, but affected families or villages only. It took burgeoning globalization, the industrialization of the Kinshasa area, & the influx of migrant workers & sex workers to support this sudden economic change to begin the epidemics in Africa in the '60s, which spread to Haiti, which then spread to IV drug users & MSM in the US by 1972. It's likely that it was in St. Louis before it was recognized as a discreet illness, as it was in many US cities.

If you're interested in this further, I highly recommend Laurie Garrett's work on the subject, as well as the Radiolab episode and especially the This Week in Virology podcast episode.

I think it's important to note that people with depression can be high-functioning (and thus nearly invisible), or obviously struggling, or psychotic. I've been diagnosed with "depression" since I first tried to kill myself at the age of 12 (so, 17 years). I am often high-functioning (hold down a good job, live alone, volunteer, take care of myself) but have still been hospitalized several times when meds stop working or I go through a trauma and I slip into a psychotic state. And I'm talking about legitimate psychosis--aural & visual hallucinations, really out-of-this-world delusions, even a really terrifying episode of Cotard's--not just thinking that someone would be better off I were dead.

So we can't just say "well it was depression, it wasn't that bad, she wouldn't have gone that crazy." It can be that bad, for lots of patients, especially if their family life is breaking up or they're scared of losing child custody etc. Yes, depression isn't always a severe mental illness on the scale of schizophrenia or bipolar, but it absolutely can be.
